title: Your First Generic Function
story: You wrote a function to print a Vec of Ints. Then you needed the same thing for Vec of Strings. And Vec of Bools. Three functions, identical except for the type. There has to be a way to write it once and reuse it for ANY type.
why: Generic functions with `[T]` let you write a single function that works with any type — eliminating duplicate code and embracing XIOM's type system.
analogy: A generic function is like a universal remote control. Instead of having separate remotes for your TV, DVD player, and sound system, one remote works with all of them. The `[T]` is like the remote saying 'I work with whatever device you point me at' — Int, Str, Bool, it doesn't matter.
try_it: Write a generic `first_element[T]` function that takes `Vec[T]` and returns `Option[T]` — the first element if it exists. Test it with Vec[Int], Vec[Str], and Vec[Bool]. Write a generic `is_empty_vec[T]` that takes `Vec[T]` and returns Bool. Notice how the function body doesn't need to know what T is — the logic works on any type.
tips: The `[T]` goes right after the function name, before the parameter list: `fn name[T](params)`
You can name your type parameter anything — `T` is convention, but `Item` or `Element` are also fine
A generic function can only do operations that work on ANY type — you can pass a T around but can't call methods specific to Int on it
common_mistakes: Forgetting the `[T]` in the function signature — without it, XIOM thinks T is a concrete type that doesn't exist
Trying to do type-specific operations inside a generic function — you can't add two T's or compare them without a constraint
Putting `[T]` on the Vec type instead of the function: `fn print(v: Vec[T])` without `[T]` on the function is an error
